chapter_title: GameObjects and Components: The Building Blocks of Unity
chapter_summary:
In Unity, everything you see and interact with in your game world is built upon two fundamental concepts: **GameObjects** and **Components**. Understanding this core architecture is paramount, as it dictates how you structure your game logic, integrate assets, and build interactive experiences. Think of a GameObject as an empty container, a placeholder in your game world. By itself, a GameObject does nothing; it has no visual representation, no physics, and no behavior. It's merely a named entity with a position, rotation, and scale in 3D space.

The magic happens when you attach **Components** to a GameObject. Components are the functional pieces that give a GameObject its properties and behaviors. They are modular scripts or built-in functionalities that you combine to create complex objects. This design philosophy is known as "composition over inheritance," a powerful paradigm where you build objects by composing them from various components rather than relying on deep, complex inheritance hierarchies. This makes your game objects highly flexible and reusable. For instance, a "Player" GameObject might have a `Mesh Renderer` component to display its 3D model, a `Capsule Collider` component for physics interaction, a `Rigidbody` component to allow it to be affected by physics, and a custom `PlayerController` script component to handle movement input.

Every single GameObject, without exception, comes with one mandatory component: the **Transform component**. This component defines the GameObject's position, rotation, and scale in the world.
*   **Position:** A `Vector3` representing the object's location in 3D space (X, Y, Z coordinates).
*   **Rotation:** A `Quaternion` (often displayed as Euler angles in the Inspector) representing the object's orientation.
*   **Scale:** A `Vector3` representing the object's size along each axis.
The Transform component is crucial because it dictates where an object is, which way it's facing, and how big it appears. When GameObjects are parented in the Hierarchy, child objects' Transforms are relative to their parent's Transform. This means if you move a parent, all its children move with it, maintaining their relative positions.

Let's look at some common built-in components you'll frequently use:
*   **Mesh Renderer:** This component works in conjunction with a `Mesh Filter` (which holds the 3D model data) to render a 3D mesh in the scene. Without a Mesh Renderer, your 3D models wouldn't be visible. It also references `Materials`, which define how the surface of the mesh looks (color, texture, shininess).
*   **Collider Components (e.g., Box Collider, Sphere Collider, Capsule Collider):** These components define the physical boundaries of an object for collision detection. They don't have a visual representation in the game itself (though they appear as green outlines in the Scene view) but are essential for physics interactions. For example, a `Box Collider` on a wall prevents the player from walking through it. There are two main types: trigger colliders (marked as "Is Trigger") which detect overlaps but don't cause physical reactions, and non-trigger colliders which do.
*   **Rigidbody:** This component enables a GameObject to be affected by Unity's physics engine. Objects with a Rigidbody can respond to gravity, forces, and collisions. If you want an object to fall, slide, or be pushed, it needs a Rigidbody. Without it, even with a Collider, an object will not react to physics. You can configure properties like `Mass`, `Drag`, `Angular Drag`, and `Is Kinematic` (which allows you to move the Rigidbody via its Transform without physics simulation). A common mistake is trying to move a Rigidbody directly by modifying its `transform.position` in `Update` instead of using `Rigidbody.MovePosition` or `Rigidbody.AddForce`, which can lead to unpredictable physics behavior.

Adding components is straightforward. Select a GameObject in the Hierarchy, then in the Inspector, click the "Add Component" button. You can then search for the desired component by name. Removing a component is equally simple: click the gear icon next to the component's name in the Inspector and select "Remove Component." You can also reorder components, though for most built-in components, the order doesn't significantly affect behavior. However, for custom scripts, the order can sometimes influence execution if one script relies on another's state in a specific lifecycle phase.

Understanding the GameObject-Component model empowers you to think modularly. Instead of creating a monolithic "Enemy" class that inherits from a "Character" class, which inherits from a "MovableObject" class, you create an "Enemy" GameObject and attach a `Mesh Renderer`, a `Capsule Collider`, a `Rigidbody`, an `EnemyAI` script, and perhaps a `Health` script. This approach promotes reusability (e.g., the `Health` script can be used on players, enemies, and destructible environmental objects) and makes your code easier to manage and extend. It's a cornerstone of efficient Unity development and crucial for gameplay programming.

screens.title: GameObjects and Components
screens.subtitle: Unity’s modular system for building every object in your scene

narration.text: In Unity, the world you build is assembled from two cooperating ideas: GameObjects and Components. A GameObject is a lightweight container — a named point in space that by itself has no visuals or behavior. Components are the modular pieces you attach to that container to give it a mesh, physics, collisions, or scripted behavior. This model encourages composition over deep inheritance so you can mix and match behaviors like LEGO pieces. For example, a single player entity can be composed by adding a Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer, a Collider for collisions, a Rigidbody for physics, and a PlayerController script for input. Practically, that means you can reuse a Health script on many different GameObjects without forcing them into an inheritance chain. As you learn these basics, you will practice adding and configuring common components, observe how the Transform component always anchors an object in space, and try a small physics lab that demonstrates Rigidbody interactions. Keep an eye out for common mistakes, like moving a physics object by writing to its Transform every frame. By the end of this lesson you will understand the building blocks that underlie every scene in Unity and how to combine them to create interactive objects.

screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you'll be able to define a GameObject and explain why it acts as a container rather than an active entity. You'll understand Components as modular building blocks that add visuals, physics, and behavior, and you'll be comfortable identifying the mandatory Transform with its position, rotation, and scale properties. Practically, you'll be able to attach and remove common built-in components such as a Mesh Renderer, Collider, or Rigidbody and configure their key properties. Finally, you'll be able to explain the principle of composition over inheritance in Unity and describe why composing behavior through components yields more reusable and flexible game objects. For example, you should be able to create a sphere, add a Rigidbody, and adjust mass and drag to change its movement, then explain why the same Health script can be reused for both enemies and players. These objectives matter because they form the foundation for scene design, predictable physics interaction, and clean code reuse across your projects.

screens.title: How you'll demonstrate mastery
screens.subtitle: Tasks, examples, and common misconceptions to check your understanding

narration.text: To demonstrate mastery you will perform several short tasks and explain your choices. First, define a GameObject in your own words and show how it changes when you attach a Mesh Renderer and a Collider. Second, attach a Rigidbody and demonstrate gravity by letting a sphere fall; explain how mass and drag influence motion using two different values. Third, manipulate a parent object's Transform and describe how children inherit relative position, highlighting the distinction between local and global coordinates. Fourth, describe a situation where composition over inheritance solves a reuse problem — for example reusing a Health script across different prefabs rather than forcing them into an inheritance chain. Watch for common misconceptions: a GameObject alone is not renderable until it has a Mesh Renderer; a Collider alone does not enable physics movement without a Rigidbody; and changing transform. position on a Rigidbody in Update can break deterministic physics. These checks will help you reason about structure and correct mistakes while creating reusable objects.

screens.title: What is a GameObject?
screens.subtitle: An empty container that becomes useful when composed with components

narration.text: A GameObject is best understood as a named container and a spatial anchor inside a Unity scene. By itself it has no mesh, no physics, and no behavior — only a Transform that stores position, rotation, and scale. That Transform determines where the GameObject exists in the world and how it relates to other objects when parented. Think of a GameObject like a blank LEGO plate: it gives you a place to attach pieces but does not define the pieces. A concrete example: when you create a Sphere primitive, Unity supplies a GameObject with a Transform, a Mesh Filter, a Mesh Renderer, and a Sphere Collider. If you remove the Mesh Renderer, the GameObject still exists but the visual disappears. A common misconception is believing a GameObject automatically does something simply because it appears in the Hierarchy. Remember, functionality comes from components. Key takeaway: treat GameObjects as flexible holders; design your scene by composing components onto them rather than relying on special-case GameObject types. What is a GameObject? means a passive container with a transform; behavior arrives only through attached components.. In practical terms, an empty container that becomes useful when composed with components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: What are Components?
screens.subtitle: Modular pieces that give a GameObject its properties and behavior

narration.text: Components are the building blocks you attach to a GameObject to give it appearance, physics, collision detection, or scripted behavior. They are intentionally modular: a single component provides one concern, like rendering or physics, and you combine many to form a complete object. For example, a playable character typically has a Mesh Filter, a Mesh Renderer, one or more Colliders, a Rigidbody if physics should apply, and scripts for movement and health logic. A clear benefit is reuse: a Health component can be attached to a player, enemy, or destructible crate without any inheritance. One misconception is thinking Components must be built-in; in Unity you can author custom script components that behave like built-ins and attach them in the same way. Practically, components can be enabled or disabled independently, removed, or reordered in the Inspector. The takeaway is to design small, focused components that do one job well, and compose them on GameObjects to create richer behavior. screens.title: Transform: Position, Rotation, Scale
screens.subtitle: How Transforms anchor objects and define parent-child relationships

narration.text: The Transform component is mandatory on every GameObject. It stores Position as a Vector3 of X, Y, Z coordinates, Rotation as a Quaternion (often shown as Euler angles in the Inspector), and Scale as a Vector3 that scales the object along each axis. Position determines where an object sits in world space; Rotation determines its orientation; Scale changes its size. Parent-child relationships modify these values: a child’s Transform is relative to its parent. For example, if an object named Arm is a child of Body and Arm has a local position of (0, 1, 0), moving Body will move Arm while keeping that local offset. A common trap is confusing local and global space — rotating the parent rotates the child because the child’s local axes rotate too. Use local coordinates when you want relative offsets and world coordinates when you need absolute positioning. Key takeaway: mastering Transform relationships is crucial for predictable motion, attaching weapons, and grouping scene objects for animation. Transform: Position, Rotation, Scale means transform defines spatial identity; parent-child relations make child transforms relative to their parent.. In practical terms, how transforms anchor objects and define parent-child relationships. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Transform properties
Position
Vector3 (X, Y, Z) — object location in space.
Rotation
Quaternion stored, Euler shown — object orientation.
Scale
Vector3 — size along axes.
Parenting behavior
Children store local transforms relative to the parent. Moving or rotating a parent affects children predictably by maintaining relative offsets.
Key Takeaway

Use local transforms for attachments and world transforms for absolute placement; remember rotation affects child axes.

Example: weapon mount
Scenario
Attach a Sword as a child of Hand. Set Sword local position so it sits correctly. When the Hand moves or rotates, the Sword follows because of the parent-child Transform relationship.
Gotcha
If you reset parent rotation unexpectedly, child local axes will change and attached objects may flip. Check both local and global values when debugging.

screens.title: Parent vs Global Coordinates
screens.subtitle: When to use local coordinates and when to use world space

narration.text: Understanding the difference between local and world coordinates prevents predictable bugs when moving or rotating grouped objects. Local coordinates express a child’s position relative to its parent; world coordinates express position relative to the scene origin. For example, a sword attached to a character's hand should use local coordinates so it maintains the correct offset as the hand animates. Conversely, to teleport a character to a fixed point in the scene you should use world coordinates. A common error is applying rotations in world space when you intend a local rotation — this can cause unexpected spins or axes misalignment. Another pitfall is computing offsets with world positions and then parenting an object, which will immediately change its apparent position because its local values differ. The concrete rule: plan whether the object should stay relative to a moving parent (use local) or remain fixed in the scene (use world). Ask yourself: do I want this object to follow its parent’s movement and rotation? If yes, use local values. Parent vs Global Coordinates means local coordinates keep relative offsets; world coordinates position objects absolutely in the scene.. In practical terms, when to use local coordinates and when to use world space. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Local coordinates keep relative offsets; world coordinates position objects absolutely in the scene.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Parent vs Global Coordinates
Comparison

Local (Parent) vs World

Local coordinates
Relative to parent. Use when an object must keep an offset from its parent, such as held items or UI attached to characters.
World coordinates
Absolute position in the scene. Use for spawning objects at fixed locations or teleporting characters.
Example & Gotcha
Scenario
Attach a lantern to a moving cart using local transform so it follows the cart. If you set world position after parenting, the lantern will jump because its local position differs.
Misconception
Using world rotation when you expect local rotation can rotate children around unexpected axes. Always confirm which space your code or transform tool uses.
Key Takeaway

Decide if an object should follow a parent; choose local for attachments and world for fixed positions.

screens.title: Mesh Filter vs Mesh Renderer
screens.subtitle: Why both are required to display a 3D model

narration.text: Rendering a 3D model in Unity typically requires two cooperating components: a Mesh Filter and a Mesh Renderer. The Mesh Filter stores the mesh geometry — the vertices, triangles, and normals that define the model. The Mesh Renderer takes that geometry and draws it using Materials that describe surface color, texture, and shading. Without the Mesh Filter, there is no model data to draw. Without the Mesh Renderer, the mesh exists but is not drawn to the screen. A practical example: import a low-poly model and add a material. The Mesh Filter holds the model; the Mesh Renderer references the material that gives it color. A common misconception is assuming a Mesh Renderer includes mesh data; it does not. Another point: Materials reference shaders and texture maps, and swapping a material changes appearance without altering geometry. Key takeaway: think of Mesh Filter as the shape and Mesh Renderer as the painter that makes that shape visible. Mesh Filter vs Mesh Renderer means mesh filter = geometry; mesh renderer = draws geometry using materials. both are required to make a model visible.. In practical terms, why both are required to display a 3d model. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Rendering rule
keyIdea.text: Mesh Filter = geometry; Mesh Renderer = draws geometry using Materials. Both are required to make a model visible.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Mesh Filter vs Mesh Renderer
Mesh Filter
Holds the mesh data: vertices, indices, normals. It is the model's geometry source.
Mesh Renderer
References Materials and shaders to draw the Mesh Filter on screen with lighting and textures.
Key Takeaway

Geometry and rendering are separate responsibilities; you usually need both for a visible model.

Example
Import a model, assign it to the Mesh Filter, then create a material and assign it to the Mesh Renderer. The object becomes visible with the chosen appearance.
Misconception
Removing the Mesh Renderer hides the mesh but does not delete mesh data from the Mesh Filter.

screens.title: Colliders: Triggers vs Solid Boundaries
screens.subtitle: How colliders define interaction volumes and the meaning of 'Is Trigger'

narration.text: Colliders define the physical boundaries used for collision detection. Common types include Box, Sphere, and Capsule Colliders. There are two primary usages: solid colliders that produce physical responses, and trigger colliders that detect overlaps without causing physical reactions. A solid collider, used alongside a Rigidbody on at least one of the colliding objects, prevents objects from passing through each other and produces collision events with physical responses. A trigger collider is marked by checking 'Is Trigger' and is used to detect when an object enters or exits a volume, often to start animations or gameplay events. For example, a door proximity detector would use a trigger collider to start an opening animation when the player enters the area. A common mistake is making the ground a trigger; this causes objects to fall through because triggers do not block physics. Another issue is expecting a Collider alone to move an object under gravity; a Rigidbody is required for gravity and force responses. Key takeaway: choose triggers for detection and solid colliders for physical blocking. Colliders: Triggers vs Solid Boundaries means use 'is trigger' for detection-only volumes; use solid colliders plus rigidbody for physical interactions and blocking.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Collider rule
keyIdea.text: Use 'Is Trigger' for detection-only volumes; use solid colliders plus Rigidbody for physical interactions and blocking.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Colliders: Triggers vs Solid Boundaries
Collider types
Box Collider
Sphere Collider
Capsule Collider
Trigger vs Solid
Trigger detects overlaps without blocking; solid colliders block physics when paired with Rigidbodies.
Key Takeaway

Use triggers for detection logic and solid colliders for physical boundaries; include Rigidbody when you want physics simulation.

Example scenarios
Door sensor: Box Collider set as Is Trigger to detect proximity and play an animation without blocking the player.
Wall: Box Collider not set as trigger so it physically blocks a player with a Rigidbody.
Gotcha
Making a collider a trigger disables its blocking behavior — objects will pass through unless you handle overlaps in code.

screens.title: Rigidbody: Physics and Common Mistakes
screens.subtitle: Enabling physics simulation and how to move objects correctly

narration.text: A Rigidbody enables a GameObject to participate in Unity’s physics simulation. With a Rigidbody attached, an object responds to gravity, collisions, forces, and torques. Rigidbody properties like Mass, Drag, and Angular Drag influence how forces affect motion. Mass determines inertia: heavier objects resist acceleration. Drag simulates air resistance, slowing a moving body. A crucial property is Is Kinematic: when true, a Rigidbody is unaffected by physics and must be moved by scripting; when false, the physics engine controls motion. A frequent mistake is moving a physics-driven object by directly setting transform. position inside Update. Doing so bypasses physics integration and leads to jitter, missed collisions, and unstable results. Instead, use Rigidbody. AddForce, Rigidbody. MovePosition in FixedUpdate, or set velocities for continuous simulation. Example: to push an object forward, call AddForce with the desired direction and magnitude, or adjust velocity if you need immediate kinematic movement. Takeaway: use Rigidbody APIs to respect Unity’s physics pipeline and avoid direct Transform changes for dynamic bodies. Rigidbody: Physics and Common Mistakes means use rigidbody for physics and move it via physics apis; avoid setting transform.position on active rigidbodies.. In practical terms, enabling physics simulation and how to move objects correctly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Physics principle
keyIdea.text: Use Rigidbody for physics and move it via physics APIs; avoid setting transform.position on active Rigidbodies.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Rigidbody: Physics and Common Mistakes
Rigidbody essentials
Mass
Controls inertia; heavier objects accelerate less under the same force.
Drag
Simulates air resistance, reducing velocity over time.
How to move
Use AddForce, AddTorque, MovePosition in FixedUpdate, or set Rigidbody.velocity for direct control. Avoid changing transform.position every frame on non-kinematic Rigidbodies.
Key Takeaway

Respect the physics pipeline: move Rigidbodies through physics methods to ensure stable, realistic interactions.

Example & Common Mistake
Example: apply Rigidbody.AddForce(Vector3.up * 10) to make an object jump. Adjust Mass and Drag to tune feel.
Common mistake
Setting transform.position every frame for a falling object breaks collision detection and produces jitter. Use physics methods instead.

screens.title: Adding and Removing Components
screens.subtitle: Use the Inspector to compose GameObjects quickly and safely

narration.text: Adding and removing components is part of daily Unity workflow and is done in the Inspector. To add a component, select the GameObject in the Hierarchy, open the Inspector, click Add Component, then search for or select the component you need. To remove a component, click the gear icon next to its header and choose Remove Component. Many built-in components can be reordered, though ordering rarely affects behavior; with custom scripts execution order may matter. Practically, test changes outside Play Mode because modifications made during Play Mode are often temporary and will revert when you stop playing. For example, if you add a Rigidbody in Play Mode and tweak mass, those changes may be lost upon exiting Play Mode. Use the Inspector to toggle components on and off to experiment without deleting them, and use component enable flags to quickly disable behavior. Takeaway: prefer making permanent configuration changes outside Play Mode and use the Inspector for rapid iteration while understanding temporary changes will revert. Adding and Removing Components means add/remove components via the inspector; avoid relying on play mode edits for permanent configuration.. In practical terms, use the inspector to compose gameobjects quickly and safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

  2. Open the Inspector and click Add Component.

Editing properties in Play Mode is useful for experimentation but will not persist after you stop playing.

screens.title: Composition over Inheritance
screens.subtitle: Why Unity favors component composition for flexible game objects

narration.text: Unity’s design emphasizes composition: build complex behavior by attaching small, focused components to GameObjects rather than creating long inheritance chains. Composition encourages reuse: a Health component can be used on players, enemies, or destructible crates without forcing them into a shared subclass. Consider an enemy and a turret: both might use the same Health script and a Damageable interface, but their movement and targeting logic differ, so separate components handle those concerns. Composition reduces coupling and avoids fragile base classes that try to do too much. One trade-off is that you must plan component responsibilities carefully to avoid scattering related logic across too many small scripts, which can make debugging harder. A practical pattern is to group related behaviors into coherent components—for example, MovementController for motion and HealthManager for damage and death. When designing, ask: does this behavior make sense being reused on other objects? If yes, it should be a standalone component rather than a subclass. Takeaway: compose responsibilities into reusable components for cleaner, more maintainable projects. Composition over Inheritance means favor small, reusable components to build objects; avoid deep inheritance hierarchies that are hard to maintain.. In practical terms, why unity favors component composition for flexible game objects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.title: Design takeaway
keyIdea.text: Favor small, reusable components to build objects; avoid deep inheritance hierarchies that are hard to maintain.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Composition over Inheritance
Why composition

Composition lets you attach independent behaviors to GameObjects so each part can be reused across different objects without forcing inheritance relationships.

Example
Enemy prefab uses Health + EnemyAI + Rigidbody + Collider. A crate can reuse Health + Collider to become destructible without duplicating AI code.
Trade-off
Too many tiny components can scatter logic. Group closely related functions sensibly.
Key Takeaway

Design components for reuse; keep responsibilities focused but not excessively fragmented.

Architecture example
Player = MovementController + HealthManager + PlayerController. Enemy = EnemyAI + HealthManager + Rigidbody. HealthManager reused across both.
Question to ask: will this behavior be useful on a different GameObject? If yes, make it a component.

screens.title: Build a Physics-Enabled Ball
screens.subtitle: Step through creating a scene, adding objects, and testing physics settings

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through creating a simple physics scene with a bouncing ball. Start a new scene and add a Plane to act as the ground, setting its Transform to (0,0,0) and scaling it to give ample area. Create a Sphere, rename it BouncingBall, and set its position to (0,5,0) so it starts above the plane. Inspect the Sphere’s default components: Transform, Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer, Sphere Collider. Next, add a Rigidbody component to the Sphere and enter Play Mode. The ball should fall and collide with the plane. While in Play Mode, experiment with Rigidbody Mass and Drag to observe different physics behaviors, but remember changes in Play Mode will revert. Exit Play Mode and set your desired Mass and Drag outside Play Mode. To test triggers, mark the Plane’s collider as Is Trigger and observe the ball falling through, illustrating that triggers do not block physics. Finally, restore Is Trigger to make the ground solid again. This activity makes concrete how Mesh, Collider, and Rigidbody combine to produce interactive physics, and shows the practical importance of editing persistent settings outside Play Mode.

keyIdea.title: Practical skill
keyIdea.text: Use the Inspector and Play Mode to test physics, but apply permanent values outside Play Mode; triggers do not block physics.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Build a Physics-Enabled Ball
Step sequence
  1. Create a new Scene and save it.
  2. GameObject → 3D Object → Plane. Set Transform to (0,0,0) and Scale to (5,1,5).
  3. GameObject → 3D Object → Sphere. Rename to BouncingBall and set Position to (0,5,0).
  4. Inspect components: add Rigidbody to the Sphere.
  5. Enter Play Mode and observe the ball fall. Adjust Mass and Drag to feel differences, then exit Play Mode and reapply permanent values.
  6. Optional: mark Plane collider as Is Trigger to observe the ball falling through, then undo to restore solid ground.
Concrete tips
Always stop Play Mode before saving permanent Rigidbody properties; Play Mode edits revert.
Use lightweight Mass values like 1 or 0.1 to test sensitivity; increase Drag to reduce sliding.
Debug
If the ball falls through, check whether the ground collider is set as a trigger or if the Rigidbody is incorrectly configured.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to carry forward

narration.text: Keep three core ideas in mind as you design scenes. First, GameObjects are containers with a mandatory Transform; they become meaningful only when you attach components. Second, Components are single-responsibility modules — Mesh Filter holds geometry, Mesh Renderer draws it, Colliders define collisions, and Rigidbody enables physics. Third, prefer composition over inheritance: attach reusable components like Health or MovementController to many different GameObjects rather than building deep class hierarchies. A quick example: both an enemy and a destructible crate can share the same Health component while having distinct movement or interaction components. These concepts together guide scene architecture, make debugging simpler, and speed up reuse across projects. Keep testing in Play Mode to explore behavior, but apply permanent changes outside Play Mode to avoid losing edits. keyIdea.title: Summary strip
keyIdea.text: GameObjects + Components + Transform + Composition form the foundation of Unity's scene organization.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Key Concepts
GameObject
A named container with a Transform; inert until composed.
Component
Modular functionality: renderer, collider, Rigidbody, or custom scripts.
Composition
Compose behaviors rather than building complex inheritance trees for reuse and flexibility.
Final takeaway

Organize scenes by composing focused components on GameObjects, use Transform relationships intentionally, and prefer reusable components over inheritance to build scalable projects.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three actionable reminders for your next scene

narration.text: Before you leave this lesson, hold on to three actionable reminders. First, always check that a GameObject has the components required for the behavior you expect — a visible model needs both Mesh Filter and Mesh Renderer, and physics needs a Rigidbody plus Colliders. Second, when tuning physics, experiment in Play Mode to observe behavior, but set final values outside Play Mode to persist changes. Third, design small, focused components that can be reused across objects; this reduces duplication and speeds iteration. For a quick test, create a sphere, add a Rigidbody, and adjust mass; then create a second sphere and reuse the same Health component to see how composition improves reuse. Keep asking whether a behavior should be reusable — if so, make it a component.
